opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something my thinking has really shifted on over the years. A lot of my earlier work in program synthesis, things like DreamCoder, was built around domain-specific languages. You'd hand-design a small language for drawing pictures, or manipulating lists, or building towers, and the system would learn to write programs in that language and even grow the language by discovering new abstractions. That's beautiful when it works, but there's always this nagging problem: somebody, usually me or a grad student, had to sit down and engineer the DSL in the first place. And that engineering smuggles in a lot of the intelligence. The DSL is doing a huge amount of the heavy lifting, and it doesn't transfer. Each new domain means designing a new language from scratch.

Python flips that around. It's a general-purpose language that can express pretty much anything you'd want: physics simulations, symbolic reasoning, string manipulation, probabilistic models, you name it. And critically, there's an enormous amount of Python out there on the internet, so large language models have absorbed a huge prior over how people actually write code to solve problems. That prior is incredibly valuable. In the old days, the search over programs was blind, or guided by a small neural network trained on a narrow distribution. Now you can lean on a model that has effectively seen millions of human solutions, and it proposes plausible programs right out of the gate.

So for me the practical argument is twofold. First, generality: I don't want to rebuild the representation every time I move to a new problem, whether that's ARC-style puzzles, learning world models for an agent, or modeling some scientific phenomenon. Second, you get to piggyback on all of that human knowledge baked into code, both through the libraries themselves and through the language models that have learned to write them.

Now, I don't think DSLs are dead. There's still a real role for learning abstractions, building up libraries of reusable concepts, and in a sense, what you want is for the system to grow its own domain-specific vocabulary on top of Python, as functions and helpers it discovers and reuses. But the substrate, the starting point, should be something broad and expressive, and Python happens to be the lingua franca for that right now. It's less about Python being elegant, frankly, and more about it being where the knowledge is.

r001.rationale: The response says DSLs require domain-specific engineering and do not transfer, but does not attribute learning difficulty to compositional complexity in Turing-complete DSLs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts hand-designed DSLs with Python’s generality, but does not connect the evolution of software-engineering language design to languages’ suitability for AI problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I actually spent a lot of my earlier career building domain-specific languages. DreamCoder, a lot of the program-synthesis work I did at MIT, was all about hand-designing a little language with the right primitives so that a search procedure could find short programs in it. And that works, but it has a hidden cost, which is that the person designing the DSL is doing a huge amount of the intellectual work up front. You're baking in what the right abstractions are, what the right primitives are, and then the system looks clever because it recombines them. If you pick a different domain, you're back to square one writing a new language.

The thing that changed my mind is partly just the existence of large language models trained on enormous amounts of Python. Python is the language where the prior is strongest. If I ask a model to write a program, it has seen millions of examples of people solving problems in Python, with all the idioms, all the libraries, all the ways of structuring things. So the "search" over programs is now guided by this incredibly rich prior that nobody had to hand-engineer. With a bespoke DSL you throw all of that away, and you have to learn or hand-specify the prior from scratch.

The second reason is expressiveness. The problems I care about, things like concept learning, learning world models, learning from a few examples the way a person would, those don't stay inside a neat little box. You start with a tidy functional language, and then you need loops, mutable state, a dictionary, a call to some library, and your DSL either grows into a bad general-purpose language or it blocks you. Python already is the general-purpose language, and it has the ecosystem. If a learned model wants to represent a physics simulation, it can just call out to a simulator. If it wants to represent a probabilistic concept, it can write a sampler. You don't have to anticipate that.

And honestly there's a practical, almost sociological point. Python is what my students write, it's what everyone can read, and it's what the tooling supports. When you want to debug what a system learned, being able to open up the program and read it as ordinary code is a big deal. Interpretability for free, basically.

Now, I don't think DSLs are dead. The place they still matter is when you need strong guarantees, or when the search space is small enough that you really can enumerate it, or when you want to force a particular inductive bias. And I'd say the right framing is that the DSL is now something the system can build itself, as a library of Python functions, rather than something I write in advance. That's kind of the DreamCoder idea again, but with Python as the substrate and the language model as the learner. So you get the abstraction-learning story without paying the price of locking yourself into a toy language.

r001.rationale: The response describes the up-front effort of designing DSL primitives and the limits of expanding a narrow language, but it does not attribute learning difficulty in Turing-complete DSLs to compositional complexity.

r002.rationale: The response explains why Python suits the speaker’s AI work, but it does not connect that suitability to the evolution of software-engineering language design.

astra-6.text:
For me, the attraction is that Python lets you work on a much broader range of problems without having to design a new language for each one. A domain-specific language can be very useful for program synthesis: you restrict the space of possible programs, and that makes search easier. But then someone has to decide what the primitives are, and those choices can encode quite a lot of the solution.

With Python, you already have a language that people use, libraries you can build on, and existing code to learn from. You can express the task and execute a candidate solution in the same environment. The tradeoff is that the search space is much bigger and messier. But that’s also part of the problem I’m interested in: how do we learn enough structure to write useful programs without having to handcraft a small language for every task?

r002.rationale: It says Python is widely used and supports a broad range of problems, but does not connect the evolution of software-engineering language design to languages’ suitability for AI problems.

sol-6.1.text:
For the problems I care about, you often don’t know ahead of time what the right abstractions are. You’re exploring the problem at the same time as you’re building the solution. Python gives you the flexibility to do that, and it lets you connect to all the machinery you need—learning libraries, numerical computation, data processing—without having to build that infrastructure yourself.

A domain-specific language can be very useful when you have a well-defined domain and you know what structure you want to exploit. But then you have to decide what the language can express. If your problem falls outside that boundary, you’re suddenly doing language design instead of solving the problem.

So I think there’s an interesting middle ground: use Python as the substrate, but learn or build specialized abstractions within it. You can get some of the advantages of a domain-specific language without committing to a closed world up front.
